description_full: Tootsie Roll Industries, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and sells confectionery products in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and internationally. The company sells its products under the Tootsie Roll, Tootsie Fruit Roll, Tootsie Pops, Tootsie Mini Pops, Child's Play, Caramel Apple Pops, Charms, Blow-Pop, Charms Mini Pops, Cella's, Dots, Junior Mints, Charleston Chew, Sugar Daddy, Sugar Babies, Andes, Fluffy Stuff, Dubble Bubble, Razzles, Cry Baby, Nik-L-Nip, And Tutsi Pop trademarks. It sells its products directly to wholesale distributors of candy, food and groceries, supermarkets, variety stores, dollar stores, chain grocers, drug chains, discount chains, cooperative grocery associations, mass merchandisers, warehouse and membership club stores, vending machine operators, e-commerce merchants, on-line marketplaces, the U.S. military and fund-raising charitable organizations, as well as through food and grocery brokers. Tootsie Roll Industries, Inc. was founded in 1896 and is headquartered in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Tootsie Roll Industries, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $2.9B market cap on $733M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 7% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 35%.

The business throws off $96M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.31× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.1%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 58% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 14% operating margin runs 7pp above the Consumer Defensive median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 5% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 14% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.41, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.34 vs 5y 0.26), so read it loosely.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $18.15 (margin of safety -115%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $14.93 to $22.87 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 30.9 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 22.1 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 30.4 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 8% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 10.0% annual cash-flow growth, 15pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 6.9%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.17).
It runs a 35% gross margin and converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.31x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $176.6M (6% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.2% over 3 years, 9.2% over 5 years and 3.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.2% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.8x depreciation (4.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders own 57.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 31%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.1% (0.2% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has grown 1.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 1.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 2,100 employees, each generates about $349K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 2.3% a year.
That works out to $46K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.2M (20x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
